classification_baseline: The cross-entropy baseline classified 1,202 of 1,512 test images correctly, giving an accuracy of 79.50%. Performance was uneven across diagnoses: recall reached 90.43% for naevi (NV), but only 60.82% for melanoma (MEL), 44.19% for actinic keratosis/intraepithelial carcinoma (AKIEC) and 42.86% for vascular lesions (VASC). Macro recall (62.75%) and macro F1 (67.35%) were consequently lower than support-weighted F1 (79.41%). The macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.9574, indicating that good probability ranking coexisted with errors at the fixed maximum-probability decision rule.
imbalance: Inverse-frequency weighted cross-entropy shifted predictions away from the dominant NV class. Macro recall increased by 7.25 percentage points to 70.00%, while accuracy decreased by 3.37 points to 76.12%. Paired 95% bootstrap intervals were 3.05 to 11.61 points for the recall increase and -5.49 to -1.19 points for the accuracy difference. Recall rose most for AKIEC (44.19% to 65.12%), dermatofibroma (DF; 63.64% to 79.55%) and VASC (42.86% to 65.71%). This broader coverage came with lower macro precision (64.31% versus 76.69%). The confusion matrices locate the cost: 161 NV images received another label, compared with 87 under the baseline. The added errors included NV images assigned to MEL (51 to 74) or benign keratosis-like lesions (BKL; 26 to 56). MEL-to-NV errors decreased from 52 to 33, although correct MEL recall increased only to 61.99% because some errors shifted to other diagnoses. Focal loss produced the highest observed MEL recall (67.84%; 116 of 171 images) and macro F1 (67.62%). Its effect was class dependent: basal cell carcinoma (BCC) recall fell to 49.46%, compared with 67.74% for the baseline and 66.67% for weighted cross-entropy. Differences between focal loss and the baseline were small overall. The accuracy difference was -0.86 points (95% interval -2.71 to 0.99), and the macro-F1 difference was 0.27 points (95% interval -3.65 to 4.26); neither interval resolved the direction of the effect. Weighted cross-entropy therefore improved average class coverage at a measurable cost in accuracy, whereas focal loss mainly redistributed errors among classes.
screening: For a research prototype that places broad lesion coverage ahead of the number of correct labels, weighted cross-entropy is the preferred candidate. It provides the highest macro recall, improves AKIEC, DF and VASC detection, and retains substantially more BCC recall than focal loss. The increased classification of NV as other diagnoses could add to clinician review workload, which was not measured here. For a melanoma-prioritized prototype, focal loss would instead be the candidate because of its higher observed MEL recall, with the accompanying BCC weakness made explicit. Even that model assigned an incorrect diagnosis to 55 of 171 MEL images. Selection therefore depends on the intended review task; these results do not establish a model for independent clinical clearance.

gradcam.analysis: The correctly classified NV image shows a central brown lesion with a darker lower focus. Activation is strongest over that focus and the central lesion, consistent with a contribution from local pigmentation and texture. A weaker upper-right background response suggests that the score may also depend on surrounding appearance. The predicted NV probability rounds to 100.00%.

In the correctly classified MEL image, blue-white and dark pigmentation varies across the lesion, with irregular margins and a brown lower extension. Activation concentrates in the lower central interior and extends towards the lower edge; the upper margin contributes less visibly. This pattern associates the MEL score with heterogeneous lesion appearance, without establishing how the complete boundary was assessed. The predicted MEL probability rounds to 100.00%.

The MEL image misclassified as NV is an unusually framed finger/nail or acral view with skin ridges and a strong vignette. NV-target activation peaks near a small dark upper-rim mark and the far-left presentation boundary, with weaker responses over much of the finger. The distribution raises the possibility of sensitivity to framing or peripheral appearance. The incorrect NV probability exceeds 99.99%, illustrating that a highly confident output can accompany a classification error.

The VASC image misclassified as MEL contains a very dark irregular centre, pale blue-white areas and peripheral redness. Activation is concentrated in the centre and along the lower lesion border. Dark pigmentation and colour variation may contribute to the MEL score, but the heatmap does not show whether vascular features were adequately represented. The incorrect MEL probability is 99.71%.

segmentation_cases.analysis: The lowest-Dice 3D case contains a substantial failure of the 3D model. At Z = 35, the annotation occupies a small image-right region, while the 3D prediction includes a large unrelated image-left structure and misses part of the annotated region. The 2D prediction is closer on this slice and over the complete volume: Dice is 86.94% versus 64.12%, and HD95 is 47.34 versus 65.81 voxels. The 3D mask contains 142,910 false-positive and 23,753 false-negative voxels, with only 54.88% of its prediction in the largest connected component. Predicted foreground volume exceeds the annotation by 69.00%, compared with 15.43% for 2D. Remote excess foreground accounts for both poor overlap and large boundary displacement; even the better 2D result retains substantial surface error.

The median-ranked 3D case illustrates improved global geometry with residual local errors. At Z = 61, both models recover much of the main annotated region but extend the image-left protrusion and incompletely reproduce a smaller separate cross-section. A small 3D false-positive spot is also visible. Complete-volume Dice is 88.17% for 3D and 67.37% for 2D, with HD95 of 12.04 and 49.05 voxels. The 3D voxel-volume bias is only 1.83%, but this small net difference combines 23,257 false-positive with 19,953 false-negative voxels. The 2D bias is 26.60%. Near-correct total volume therefore conceals errors in shape and continuity.

The highest-Dice 3D case has 94.00% complete-volume Dice and an HD95 of 3.32 voxels, yet its selected slice contains a local omission. At Z = 66, the model follows the larger central cross-section but misses the small image-left annotated region and slightly extends an upper-right structure. There are 415 false-negative voxels on this slice. The 2D prediction captures more of the left cross-section locally, but its complete-volume Dice is lower (91.16%) and HD95 is much higher (32.77 voxels). Inspection of the full 2D mask identifies 14 connected components, with 3.30% of its predicted voxels outside the largest component and its greatest false-positive burden at Z = 16. These remote errors explain why a favourable slice can coexist with poor full-volume surface distance.

The case with the highest remaining 3D HD95 shows connected overgrowth. At Z = 33, both models include a large image-left structure outside the annotation; 3D also extends beyond the small annotated cross-section, while 2D expands both visible regions more extensively. Complete-volume Dice is 78.34% for 3D and 67.22% for 2D, with HD95 of 40.42 and 50.93 voxels. Foreground volume exceeds the annotation by 22.68% and 75.62%, respectively, corresponding to 60,651 and 141,965 false-positive voxels. For 3D, 99.69% of predicted voxels belong to one component. The error is therefore largely an expansion of the main predicted structure, which would persist after removal of small isolated components. The reported masks were evaluated without such correction.

comparison: Across the same 20 test volumes, 3D U-Net achieved a mean Dice of 86.54%, compared with 81.96% for 2D U-Net, a difference of 4.59 percentage points. Mean Jaccard was 76.89% versus 70.14%; symmetric average surface distance was 3.34 versus 8.07 voxels, and HD95 was 14.17 versus 36.16 voxels. The 3D model had higher Dice in 15 of 20 cases and lower HD95 in 17, with no empty-mask failures in either model. Neighbouring slices provide information about continuity and can help distinguish structures with similar appearance on one slice. The LA-TE13 failure shows that the same context can accompany a coherent but incorrect foreground region. The comparison also includes architectural and computational differences: 3D U-Net has 5.65 million parameters, versus 1.94 million for 2D, and training completed 9,000 versus 12,000 updates with batch sizes of 1 and 16. Observed training times were 6.67 and 26.56 minutes; complete-volume inference averaged 0.22 and 0.40 seconds. These timings include data preparation and shared GPU workload. The sequential reconstruction of 88 slices contributes to the 2D inference time. Shared data, preprocessing, loss and validation rules support a comparison of the implemented pipelines, but do not isolate dimensionality from model size, voxel exposure or computational cost.
limitations: The principal limits are the small validation sets, incomplete spatial metadata and one training seed per model. Segmentation used 11 fitting and 3 validation volumes; classification validation included only one DF and three VASC images. Patient or lesion independence across splits could not be fully verified. Image-level bootstrap intervals therefore describe sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted models and observed class supports, and may underestimate uncertainty when images are correlated. They do not capture retraining variability. The MRI axes were inferred from the source preprocessing convention, while physical spacing, anatomical orientation and direct conversion provenance remain unavailable. Possible upstream annotation-dependent cropping further limits inference to the supplied fields of view. The additional checkpoint-selection experiment was designed after inspection of the original test results and remains exploratory. Display cases illustrate selected success and failure patterns rather than their prevalence. Grad-CAM is a coarse association map, and neither expert anatomical review nor clinical workflow validation was performed. Re-evaluation in a clean directory reproduced the saved predictions and core metrics, supporting computational reproducibility within the tested environment.
selection_sensitivity: Selecting checkpoints by validation macro F1 and imposing a 20-epoch training floor changed the weighted cross-entropy result without yielding an overall improvement. Its selected epoch moved from 2 to 18, and validation macro F1 rose from 74.76% to 80.97%. On the test set, macro F1 increased by only 0.93 percentage points, from 66.16% to 67.09%, while accuracy declined from 76.12% to 75.93% and macro recall from 70.00% to 64.50%. AKIEC and DF recall fell from 65.12% and 79.55% to 44.19% and 54.55%. Cross-entropy and focal loss retained epochs 5 and 16 and the same discrete test accuracy, recall and F1 as their original runs. The three supplementary runs completed 20, 28 and 26 epochs. The altered selection rule therefore favoured a different weighted-loss tradeoff but did not resolve the validation-to-test discrepancy or exceed the baseline across metrics. Because the experiment was designed after observing the test comparison and changes both training duration and selection, confirmation would require matched seeds and an untouched test set.
anatomical_interpretation: Segmentation errors could alter the apparent size and shape of the left atrial cavity before ablation. Excess foreground may enlarge the cavity or create an apparent branch, whereas omissions may shorten or narrow small extensions. The clearest excess-volume failure is LA-TE13, where the 3D mask exceeds the annotation by 69.00% and includes a remote component. In LA-TE12, largely connected overgrowth produces biases of 22.68% for 3D and 75.62% for 2D. Conversely, the highest-Dice 3D case still misses a small annotated cross-section. Such omissions could matter if they involve an inlet or appendage region, but the supplied orientation and labels do not establish those anatomical identities. The binary annotations delineate a cavity with limited extensions, without separate wall or ostial labels. Their errors concern geometric representation; they cannot establish fibrosis, thrombus or ablation targets. [7,13]

The 3D model is the stronger candidate for a supervised anatomical-modelling research workflow because it improves both average overlap and surface distance on this test set. Its advantage is present in 15 of 20 Dice comparisons and 17 HD95 comparisons. The median-ranked case illustrates the practical distinction: Dice rises from 67.37% to 88.17%, and HD95 falls from 49.05 to 12.04 voxels, while a detached prediction island remains visible in 3D. A reviewer would still need to inspect the complete surface and relevant extensions, then correct or reject inaccurate masks. The severe LA-TE13 failure would require substantial correction and favours the 2D model for that individual volume. Neither correction time nor clinical decisions were evaluated, so the observed geometric advantage does not establish a workflow benefit.

Clinical deployment would require independent patient-level evaluation across centres, scanners, acquisition protocols and image quality. Original spatial geometry and full fields of view should be restored, because the supplied pre-cropped arrays cannot establish performance on routine scans. Multiple experts should annotate and independently review the same cases, including anatomical variants, low-quality scans and examples of the failure patterns observed here. Assessment should cover volume bias, inlet and extension geometry, surface completeness, case rejection and correction time in addition to overlap. A failure detector would need validation without access to the reference mask. A prospective assisted-workflow study should then measure how clinicians use the outputs, resolve disagreements and handle unacceptable predictions. External, inter-reader and prospective workflow validation were beyond the present experiments.
